result.relation_rationale: The requested four-month ability-to-work comparison is reported in the main text under “Return to work.” The study defines workability as having a job, being in school, or seeking work. The analyzed population is restricted to those returning for follow-up (45 treated and 49 control participants), not all 106 randomized participants. Follow-up is described as four months after graduation for treated participants, with matched intervals for controls.

Statistical methods
The baseline and 4-month values were compared
in separate analyses using Mann-Whitney tests. Be-
cause more patients in the treated group were able
to work at baseline, an additional Fisher-Irwin test
was done for this parameter. The level of signifi-
cance was defined as 5%.
The results are based on data collected at a fol-
low-up examination at 4 months (the first Monday
after 122 days after graduation). Each patient in the
control group was matched at randomization with
one in the treated group, so that the interval be-
tween the initial medical examination and the 4-
month examination was identical.
Return to work
One of the major goals of the project was to
prepare patients physically and psychologically to go
back to work. "Workability" was defined as having a
job, being in school, or seeking work.
At the 4-month follow-up, 29 (64%) of the 45
treated patients were able to work, compared with
12 (27%) at baseline; in the control group, 14
(28%) of the 49 patients were able to work at the
time of the 4-month follow-up, compared with 8
(16%) at baseline. The difference between the two
groups was significant (P < .001); the differences in
the before and after values in the two groups were
also significant (P < .001 by Fisher-Irwin test). Of
the 29 patients able to work in the treated group, 17
had full-time jobs, seven were unemployed but seek-
ing work, and five were in school. Of the patients in
the treated group who could not work, six were
receiving social pensions and the rest were still on
sick leave. In the control group, 10 of the 14 pa-
tients able to work were working full-time, three
were unemployed but seeking work, and one was in
school. Eight persons in this group were receiving
social pensions and the rest were on sick leave.
Health care, sick leave
The treated group contacted family doctors, spe-
cialists, physical therapists, chiropractors, or hospi-
tals significantly fewer times than the control group
did. They also used significantly fewer days of sick
leave (Table 3).
Pain and function
Patients used a scale of 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst
possible pain) to rate pain in the back and in the
legs. After 4 months, the treated group had signifi-
cantly less back pain than the controls, but they had
no difference in leg pain (Table 3).

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

6|BACKGROUND
7|Americans with low back pain have been helped to
8|return to work by multidisciplinary intensive treatment programs.
9|Whether this treatment method will succeed in countries with a
10|more generous social welfare system, where the incentive to re-
11|turn to work might be less, is not proven.
12|To evaluate a Danish program of functional restora-
13|tion combined with behavioral support.
14|•fliai:!»:»« Patients who had experienced at least 6 months of dis-
15|abling low back pain were randomly assigned to either a 3-week
16|intensive treatment program (n = 55) or an untreated control group
17|(n = 51).
18|Of the 106 patients randomized, 94 (89%) returned
19|for a 4-month follow-up visit. At that time, 29 (64%) of the
20|45 treated patients were able to work, compared with 14 of 49
21|(29%) in the control group. The treated patients had used
22|fewer days of sick leave (P < .02), had contacted health care
23|professionals fewer times (P < .001), and had lower pain and
24|disability scores.

answers.justification: The approved result is ability to work, comparing assignment to a 3-week intensive multidisciplinary program with untreated control, at four-month follow-up (4 months after graduation for treated participants, matched intervals for controls); the reported figures are among returnees, not all randomized participants. The report says the study was observer-blinded: the examining physician did not know group assignment, but it does not say participants were blinded. Participants received a conspicuous intensive program compared with no treatment, making participant awareness probable, though no direct statement establishes their knowledge.
unknowns: No direct report establishes participant blinding or their knowledge of allocation.

counterevidence.implication: The only expressly described blinding was the observer/examining physician, and it was broken when some participants disclosed their group; this leaves participant blinding unreported rather than establishing participant knowledge.

answers.justification: The intensive program and untreated control were visibly different; delivery involved a structured 39-hour-per-week program. This supports probable awareness by those delivering it, but the report does not directly state whether intervention personnel were blinded.
unknowns: No explicit report of allocation concealment or blinding/awareness among intervention personnel.

counterevidence.implication: The report specifically identifies blinding of the follow-up physician, not the intervention providers; it does not directly document provider awareness.

answers.justification: The report documents ordinary noncompletion: two assigned treatment participants never started (one developed disk herniation, one did not appear), and seven dropped out, citing treatment difficulty, increased pain and other reasons. However, it gives no protocol against which to classify these as inconsistent deviations and no evidence that trial recruitment, research-only engagement or trial personnel caused them beyond circumstances that could occur in ordinary treatment. Control patients were not treated by the study and could seek treatment elsewhere, but no prohibited crossovers or context-caused departures are reported. Thus neither protocol inconsistency nor the required trial-context causal link is established.
unknowns: Protocol requirements and permissions concerning non-initiation, discontinuation, and outside treatment are not reported.
No documented reason links deviations to trial-specific engagement or personnel decisions.

limitations.premise: Whether non-initiation, treatment discontinuation, or outside control-group treatment was inconsistent with the protocol and caused by trial context remains unresolved.
limitations.stopping_rationale: The complete captured main report was read. answers.justification: The intended effect is assignment among all randomized participants, but the reported workability comparison uses only 45 treated and 49 control participants returning at four months; the report expressly excludes the two who never started and seven dropouts from analysis except that only two were contacted. These are eligible randomized participants omitted because they did not complete/return, not merely participants with missing outcome data in an otherwise assignment analysis. Hence this is not an appropriate analysis estimating the approved assignment effect. The returnees' observed values and comparison remain as reported; no reinterpretation of the Result as an all-randomized estimate is made.
unknowns: The report does not provide outcomes for the omitted randomized participants.

counterevidence.implication: The analyzed comparison preserves original treatment/control groups and matched follow-up intervals among returnees, but the restricted post-randomization population is not the full randomized assignment population.

answers.justification: Although 9 of 106 randomized participants (including two never-started) were excluded from the reported analysis and only two of those nine were reachable at four months, the endpoint was common among returnees (29/45 and 14/49). The excluded treatment participants included people who never appeared, had disk herniation, found the program too difficult or could not accept increased pain; returnees' outcomes do not establish omitted participants' workability. Given exclusion due to treatment non-initiation/dropout and reasons plausibly related to prognosis or ability to work, the assignment contrast could be materially affected, but outcome status and exact effect among those excluded are unknown.
unknowns: Workability outcomes for the excluded participants and the extent their exclusion would alter the result are unknown.

counterevidence.implication: The outcome was not rare among analyzed returnees, and nine participants comprise a minority of the 106 randomized; nevertheless the exclusions may be prognostically related and their outcomes are unavailable.

answers.justification: The approved result is ability to work, comparing assignment to a 3-week intensive multidisciplinary program with untreated control, at four-month follow-up (4 months after graduation for treated participants, matched intervals for controls); reported figures are among returnees, not all randomized. Report says observer-blinded: examining physician did not know assignment, but does not say participants blinded. Participants received a conspicuous intensive program versus no treatment, making awareness probable though not directly established.
unknowns: No direct report establishes participant blinding or knowledge of allocation.

counterevidence.implication: Only examiner blinding is expressly described, and that was sometimes broken by participant disclosure; this does not directly establish participant knowledge.

answers.justification: The intensive program and untreated control were visibly different; delivery involved a structured 39-hour-per-week program. This supports probable awareness by those delivering it, but the report does not directly state whether intervention personnel were blinded.
unknowns: No explicit report of allocation concealment or blinding/awareness among intervention personnel.

counterevidence.implication: The report specifically identifies follow-up physician blinding, not intervention providers; provider awareness is not directly documented.

answers.justification: The report documents noncompletion: two assigned treatment participants never started (one developed disk herniation, one did not appear), and seven dropped out, citing treatment difficulty, increased pain and other reasons. Controls could seek treatment elsewhere, but no prohibited crossovers or context-caused departures are reported. Neither protocol inconsistency nor trial-context causation is established.

answers.justification: The approved assignment effect targets all randomized participants, while workability comparison uses only 45 treated and 49 control returnees; the report expressly excludes the two who never started and seven dropouts from analysis except that only two were contacted. These eligible randomized participants were omitted due to noncompletion/nonreturn, not merely missing outcomes in an assignment analysis. Thus this is not an appropriate analysis estimating the approved assignment effect. The returnees' comparison remains as reported; it is not reinterpreted as an all-randomized estimate.

counterevidence.implication: The analyzed comparison preserves treatment/control groups and matched intervals among returnees, but remains restricted post-randomization.

answers.justification: Nine of 106 randomized participants (including two never-started) were excluded; only two of those nine were reachable at four months. Workability was common among returnees (29/45 and 14/49), but excluded treatment participants included people who never appeared, had disk herniation, found the program too difficult, or could not accept increased pain. Their workability is unknown; exclusions plausibly relate to prognosis or ability to work, so the assignment contrast could be materially affected, though its magnitude is not determined.
unknowns: Workability outcomes for excluded participants and resulting impact are unknown.

counterevidence.implication: Outcome was common in returnees and nine participants are a minority of 106, though their outcomes are unknown and exclusion reasons may be prognostic.
